title: No. 22 — The Same Subject Continued (Other Defects of the Present Confederation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: In addition to the defects already enumerated in the existing federal system, there are others of no less importance, which together make it altogether unfit for the administration of the affairs of the Union.

The lack of a power to regulate commerce is admitted by all parties to be one of them. The usefulness of such a power has been anticipated under the first head of our inquiries, and for that reason, as well as from the universal conviction held on the subject, little needs to be added here. It is indeed obvious, on the most superficial view, that there is no object, whether for trade or finance, that more strongly demands a federal supervision. The lack of it has already blocked the formation of beneficial treaties with foreign powers, and has given rise to dissatisfaction between the States. No nation acquainted with the nature of our political association would be unwise enough to enter into stipulations with the United States by which they granted privileges of any importance, while they were aware that the engagements on the part of the Union might at any moment be violated by its members, and while they found from experience that they could enjoy every advantage they wanted in our markets without granting us any return except such as their momentary convenience might suggest. It is no surprise, therefore, that Mr. Jenkinson, in introducing into the House of Commons a bill for regulating the temporary intercourse between the two countries, prefaced its introduction by declaring that similar provisions in earlier bills had been found to answer every purpose for the commerce of Great Britain, and that it would be prudent to persist in the plan until it should appear whether the American government was likely to acquire greater consistency.(1)

Several States have tried, by separate prohibitions, restrictions, and exclusions, to influence the conduct of that kingdom in this matter. But the lack of concert, arising from the lack of a general authority and from clashing and dissimilar views in the State, has so far frustrated every experiment of the kind, and will keep doing so as long as the same obstacles to a uniformity of measures continue to exist.

The interfering and unneighborly regulations of some States, contrary to the true spirit of the Union, have on different occasions given just cause for offense and complaint to others. It is to be feared that examples of this nature, if not restrained by national control, would multiply and extend until they became no less serious sources of animosity and discord than they are injurious obstacles to commerce between the different parts of the Confederacy. "The commerce of the German empire(2) is in continual difficulty from the multiplicity of the duties which the several princes and states exact upon the merchandise passing through their territories, by which the fine streams and navigable rivers with which Germany is so happily watered are rendered almost useless." Though the genius of the people of this country might never let this description strictly apply to us, we may reasonably expect, from the gradual conflicts of State regulations, that the citizens of each would eventually come to be considered and treated by the others as little better than foreigners and aliens.

The power of raising armies, by the most obvious construction of the articles of Confederation, is merely a power of making requisitions on the States for quotas of men. This practice, in the course of the late war, was found full of obstructions to a vigorous and economical system of defense. It gave rise to a competition between the States that created a kind of auction for men. To furnish the quotas required of them, they outbid each other until bounties grew to an enormous and unsupportable size. The hope of a still further increase encouraged those willing to serve to delay their enlistment, and made them unwilling to engage for any considerable period. Hence the slow and scanty levies of men in the most critical emergencies of our affairs; short enlistments at unparalleled expense; continual fluctuations in the troops, ruinous to their discipline and frequently subjecting public safety to the perilous crisis of a disbanded army. Hence also those oppressive expedients for raising men that were resorted to on several occasions, which nothing but the enthusiasm of liberty could have made the people endure.

This method of raising troops is no less unfriendly to economy and vigor than it is to an equal distribution of the burden. The States near the seat of war, driven by motives of self-preservation, made efforts to furnish their quotas that even exceeded their abilities, while those at a distance from danger were for the most part as remiss as the others were diligent in their efforts. The immediate pressure of this inequality was not, in this case, as in the case of money contributions, eased by the hope of a final settlement. The States that did not pay their proportions of money could at least be charged with their deficiencies; but no account could be made of the deficiencies in the supplies of men. We will not, however, see much reason to regret the lack of this hope, when we consider how little prospect there is that the most delinquent States will ever be able to make compensation for their financial failures. The system of quotas and requisitions, whether applied to men or money, is in every view a system of weakness in the Union, and of inequality and injustice among the members.

The right of equal suffrage among the States is another objectionable part of the Confederation. Every idea of proportion and every rule of fair representation joins to condemn a principle that gives to Rhode Island an equal weight in the scale of power with Massachusetts, or Connecticut, or New York, and to Delaware an equal voice in the national deliberations with Pennsylvania, or Virginia, or North Carolina. Its operation contradicts the fundamental maxim of republican government, which requires that the sense of the majority should prevail. Sophistry may reply that sovereigns are equal, and that a majority of the votes of the States will be a majority of confederated America. But this kind of logical sleight of hand will never counteract the plain suggestions of justice and common-sense. It may happen that this majority of States is a small minority of the people of America;(3) and two-thirds of the people of America could not long be persuaded, on the strength of artificial distinctions and syllogistic subtleties, to submit their interests to the management and disposal of one-third. The larger States would after a while revolt against the idea of receiving the law from the smaller. To accept such a deprivation of their due importance in the political scale would be not only insensitive to the love of power, but even to sacrifice the desire of equality. It is neither rational to expect the first nor just to require the second. The smaller States, considering how peculiarly their safety and welfare depend on union, ought readily to give up a pretension that, if not relinquished, would prove fatal to its duration.

It may be objected that not seven but nine States, or two-thirds of the whole number, must consent to the most important resolutions, and so it might be inferred that nine States would always include a majority of the Union. But this does not address the impropriety of an equal vote between States of the most unequal size and population. Nor is the inference accurate in fact, for we can name nine States that contain less than a majority of the people;(4) and it is constitutionally possible that these nine may give the vote. Besides, there are matters of considerable importance decided by a bare majority. There are others on which doubts have been raised, which, if interpreted in favor of the sufficiency of a vote of seven States, would extend its operation to interests of the first magnitude. In addition to this, it is to be observed that there is a probability of an increase in the number of States, with no provision for a proportional increase in the ratio of votes.

But this is not all. What at first sight may seem a remedy is in reality a poison. To give a minority a veto over the majority — which is always the case where more than a majority is required for a decision — tends to subject the sense of the greater number to that of the lesser. Congress, from the absence of a few States, has frequently been in the situation of a Polish diet, where a single VOTE has been enough to halt all their movements. A sixtieth part of the Union, which is about the proportion of Delaware and Rhode Island, has several times been able to put a complete stop to its operations. This is one of those refinements which in practice has the opposite effect to what is expected from it in theory. The necessity of unanimity in public bodies, or of something approaching it, has been founded on the supposition that it would contribute to security. But its real operation is to embarrass the administration, destroy the energy of the government, and substitute the pleasure, caprice, or artifices of an insignificant, turbulent, or corrupt junto for the regular deliberations and decisions of a respectable majority. In those emergencies of a nation in which the goodness or badness, the weakness or strength of its government is of the greatest importance, there is commonly a need for action. The public business must somehow go forward. If a stubborn minority can control the opinion of a majority on the best mode of conducting it, the majority, in order that something may be done, must conform to the views of the minority. Thus the sense of the smaller number will overrule that of the greater, and give a tone to the national proceedings. Hence tedious delays; continual negotiation and intrigue; contemptible compromises of the public good. And yet, in such a system, it is even fortunate when such compromises can be reached. On some occasions things will not admit of accommodation, and then the measures of government must be either harmfully suspended or fatally defeated. It is often kept in a state of inaction by the impossibility of obtaining the concurrence of the necessary number of votes. Its situation must always smack of weakness, sometimes border on anarchy.

It is not difficult to see that a principle of this kind gives greater scope to foreign corruption, as well as to domestic faction, than one that lets the sense of the majority decide; though the contrary has been presumed. The mistake comes from not paying due attention to the mischiefs that may be caused by obstructing the progress of government at certain critical moments. When the agreement of a large number is required by the Constitution for any national act, we tend to feel safe, because nothing improper is likely TO BE DONE. But we forget how much good may be prevented, and how much harm may be produced, by the power of hindering what is necessary, and of keeping affairs in the same unfavorable posture in which they may happen to stand at particular periods.

Suppose, for instance, we were engaged in a war along with one foreign nation against another. Suppose the necessity of our situation demanded peace, and the interest or ambition of our ally led him to want the war prosecuted with views that might justify our making separate terms. In such a state of things, this ally of ours would clearly find it much easier, by his bribes and intrigues, to tie the hands of government from making peace, where two-thirds of all the votes were required for that object, than where a simple majority would suffice. In the first case he would have to corrupt a smaller number; in the second, a larger. On the same principle, it would be much easier for a foreign power with which we were at war to confuse our councils and embarrass our efforts. And in a commercial view, we may be subjected to similar inconveniences. A nation with which we had a treaty of commerce could with much greater ease prevent our forming a connection with her competitor in trade, however beneficial such a connection might be to ourselves.

Evils of this kind ought not to be regarded as imaginary. One of the weak sides of republics, among their numerous advantages, is that they offer too easy an entry to foreign corruption. A hereditary monarch, though often inclined to sacrifice his subjects to his ambition, has so great a personal interest in the government and in the external glory of the nation that it is not easy for a foreign power to give him an equivalent for what he would sacrifice by treachery to the state. The world has accordingly seen few examples of this kind of royal prostitution, though there have been abundant specimens of every other kind.

In republics, men raised from the mass of the community by the votes of their fellow-citizens to stations of great pre-eminence and power may find compensations for betraying their trust which, except to minds animated and guided by superior virtue, may seem to exceed the proportion of interest they have in the common stock, and to outweigh the obligations of duty. That is why history furnishes us with so many mortifying examples of the prevalence of foreign corruption in republican governments. How much this contributed to the ruin of the ancient commonwealths has already been described. It is well known that the deputies of the United Provinces have on various occasions been bought by the agents of neighboring kingdoms. The Earl of Chesterfield (if my memory serves), in a letter to his court, hints that his success in an important negotiation must depend on his obtaining a major's commission for one of those deputies. And in Sweden the parties were alternately bought by France and England in so brazen and notorious a manner that it caused universal disgust in the nation, and was a principal cause that the most limited monarch in Europe, in a single day, without tumult, violence, or opposition, became one of the most absolute and uncontrolled.

One circumstance that crowns the defects of the Confederation remains to be mentioned: the lack of a judiciary power. Laws are a dead letter without courts to expound and define their true meaning and operation. The treaties of the United States, to have any force at all, must be considered part of the law of the land. Their true meaning, as it concerns individuals, must, like all other laws, be settled by judicial determinations. To produce uniformity in these determinations, they ought to be submitted, in the last resort, to one SUPREME TRIBUNAL. And this tribunal ought to be set up under the same authority that forms the treaties themselves. Both ingredients are indispensable. If there is in each State a court of final jurisdiction, there may be as many different final determinations on the same point as there are courts. The opinions of men differ endlessly. We often see not only different courts, but the judges of the same court, differing from each other. To avoid the confusion that would inevitably result from the contradictory decisions of a number of independent courts, all nations have found it necessary to establish one court paramount to the rest, possessing a general superintendence and authorized to settle and declare in the last resort a uniform rule of civil justice.

This is the more necessary where the frame of the government is so compounded that the laws of the whole are in danger of being contravened by the laws of the parts. In this case, if the particular tribunals are given a right of ultimate jurisdiction, besides the contradictions to be expected from differences of opinion, there will be much to fear from the bias of local views and prejudices, and from the interference of local regulations. As often as such interference happened, there would be reason to fear that the provisions of the particular laws might be preferred to those of the general laws. Nothing is more natural to men in office than to look with peculiar deference toward that authority to which they owe their official existence.

The treaties of the United States, under the present Constitution, are liable to violation by thirteen different legislatures, and by as many different courts of final jurisdiction acting under the authority of those legislatures. The faith, the reputation, the peace of the whole Union are thus continually at the mercy of the prejudices, the passions, and the interests of every member of which it is composed. Is it possible that foreign nations can either respect or trust such a government? Is it possible that the people of America will any longer consent to trust their honor, their happiness, their safety, on so precarious a foundation?

In this review of the Confederation, I have confined myself to laying out its most material defects, passing over those imperfections in its details by which even much of the power intended to be conferred on it has been largely rendered ineffective. By this time it must be evident to all reflective men, who can free themselves from preconceived opinions, that it is a system so radically vicious and unsound that it admits not of amendment but only of an entire change in its leading features and characters.

The organization of Congress is itself utterly improper for the exercise of those powers that need to be deposited in the Union. A single assembly may be a proper receptacle of those slender, or rather fettered, authorities heretofore delegated to the federal head. But it would be inconsistent with all the principles of good government to entrust it with those additional powers which even the moderate and more rational adversaries of the proposed Constitution admit ought to reside in the United States. If that plan should not be adopted, and if the necessity of the Union should be able to withstand the ambitious aims of those men who may indulge magnificent schemes of personal aggrandizement from its dissolution, the probability is that we should run into the project of conferring supplementary powers on Congress as it is now constituted. Either the machine, from the intrinsic feebleness of its structure, will crumble into pieces despite our ill-judged efforts to prop it up; or, by successive augmentations of its force and energy as necessity might prompt, we will finally accumulate, in a single body, all the most important prerogatives of sovereignty, and so entail on our posterity one of the most execrable forms of government that human delusion ever contrived. Thus we should create in reality the very tyranny which the adversaries of the new Constitution either are, or pretend to be, anxious to avert.

It has not a little contributed to the infirmities of the existing federal system that it never had a ratification by the PEOPLE. Resting on no better foundation than the consent of the several legislatures, it has been exposed to frequent and intricate questions about the validity of its powers, and has, in some cases, given rise to the enormous doctrine of a right of legislative repeal. Owing its ratification to the law of a State, it has been argued that the same authority might repeal the law by which it was ratified. However gross a heresy it may be to maintain that a PARTY to a COMPACT has a right to revoke that COMPACT, the doctrine itself has had respectable advocates. The mere possibility of such a question proves the necessity of laying the foundations of our national government deeper than the mere sanction of delegated authority. The fabric of American empire ought to rest on the solid basis of THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE. The streams of national power ought to flow immediately from that pure, original fountain of all legitimate authority.
